name: The Caucasian Elm of Square Samuel Paty
age_estimate: not documented for this individual; the species itself was introduced to Paris in 1782, which is context about the species, not this tree's planting date

location.address: Square Samuel Paty, 3 Place Paul Painleve, 75005 Paris
location.neighbourhood: Latin Quarter, opposite the Sorbonne, 5th arrondissement

access: Free, open public square, no closure found
transport: Cluny-La Sorbonne (Metro 10) or Maubert-Mutualite (Metro 10), 3-4 min walk
story: Paris lost most of its elms to a fungus, and this one survived by not quite being an elm. Zelkova carpinifolia is a Caucasian cousin of the true elms, native to the mountains between the Black Sea and the Caspian, and it is far less susceptible to the Dutch elm disease that emptied streets across Europe. That is the reason a tree of this size still stands in the middle of the Latin Quarter. The city register gives it a girth of 267 centimetres and a height of 20 metres, and gives no age at all. Nor does any other source. The species first reached Paris in 1782, but that is a date about the species, not about this trunk, and nothing documents when this one was planted. It stands in the small square facing the Sorbonne across Place Paul Painleve, with the Musee de Cluny and the Roman baths under it a minute away, on ground students have crossed on their way to lectures for as long as the tree has been there. In 2021 the Paris Council renamed the square for Samuel Paty, the history and geography teacher murdered in 2020. The tree kept its address and lost the old name, which is the sort of thing a long-lived tree tends to do more than once.

name: The Oriental Planes of Square Michel-Foucault
age_estimate: not documented; register gives girth only (470cm and 415cm for the two trees)

location.address: Square Michel-Foucault, 43 Rue des Ecoles, 75005 Paris
location.neighbourhood: Latin Quarter, opposite the College de France, 5th arrondissement

access: Free, open public square, no closure found
transport: Maubert-Mutualite (Metro 10) or Cluny-La Sorbonne, 3-5 min walk
story: Two oriental planes stand a few metres apart here, one measuring 470 centimetres around the trunk and the other 415. That is nearly nine metres of girth between them in a pocket garden of roughly 2,000 square metres, which is why they are listed here as one entry rather than two: you stand in a single spot and look up at both. Neither has a documented age. The city register records their girth and nothing more, no source gives a planting date, and large and old is as far as the evidence honestly goes. For scale, the thickest plane in Paris, in Parc Monceau, measures eight metres around and was planted in 1814, and the Parc Montsouris plane reaches 605 centimetres and dates from 1840. These two sit below those and above almost everything else in the city. The garden faces the College de France across Rue des Ecoles and takes its name from Michel Foucault, who lectured in the building opposite. It was renamed for him in 2005, long after these trunks were full grown. A bronze Dante by Jean-Paul Aube stands beneath them, and the two planes shade a steady traffic of students, visitors walking up to the Musee de Cluny and people eating lunch on the slope.

name: The Plane of Quai Saint-Bernard
age_estimate: not documented for this individual specimen; the register gives girth (380cm) only

location.address: Quai Saint-Bernard, near Jardin Tino-Rossi, 75005 Paris
location.neighbourhood: Left Bank of the Seine, near the Jardin des Plantes, 5th arrondissement

access: Free, open riverside quay and sculpture garden (Jardin Tino-Rossi), no closure found
transport: Gare d'Austerlitz (Metro 5/10, RER C) or Jussieu (Metro 7/10), 5-8 min walk along the river
story: The sculptures are the newcomers. The Jardin Tino-Rossi was laid out along the Seine in 1980 as an open-air museum of modern sculpture, and it was built around plane trees that were already standing: the garden's own record notes old planes on the site before the garden existed. One of them is on the city's register of remarkable trees, on Quai Saint-Bernard, with a girth of 380 centimetres. Which of them, precisely, is where this entry has to be careful. The register lists a plane of that size at this point on the quay and gives a position for it. A second source confirms that old planes genuinely stand here, but nothing beyond the register singles out this trunk from the others along the same walk. By that listing it is the registered tree; by any other evidence available it is one large plane among several, and no planting date is documented for any of them. That is still a good reason to walk this stretch. The quay runs below the Jardin des Plantes towards the Institut du Monde Arabe, the river on one side and bronze and stone works standing free in the grass on the other. The planes are the oldest things in the garden and the only part of it nobody designed.
